title: State of ai question
author: Kitchen-Turnip6356
selftext:
If you are using ainto its potential In 2026 what would that say for your work flows?

  
Essentially im trying to see if im caught up and being as productive as possible. What is the current state of ai game dev? What should everyone know?

comments.author: _HoundOfJustice
comments.body: Are you talking specifically about AI heavy game devs or game devs who use generative AI here and there and not as their entire workflow? I personally rely on industry standard tools and pipeline (Photoshop, 3ds Max, Maya, ZBrush, Substance package, Marvelous Designer and some other tools i rely on) with generative AI as yet another tool i added and use here and there for the one or another purpose. If you are only interested in AI game dev as in relying on generative AI workflow then im not supposed to answer further here, if you ask about generally game development with generative AI being involved but not as heavy lifter then its a different story.

replies.author: Kitchen-Turnip6356
replies.body: No im just wondering what the common and proper uses for it are and if im missing out on any work flows. Im not just trying to only use ai

replies.author: _HoundOfJustice
replies.body: Outside of AI circles serious game developers usually use generative AI for smaller tasks like ideations for their game design or assets as well as some coding tasks. Thats typical and im one of them. My advantage is that im a professional artist and neither do i need to rely on AI nor pay other pros to make all the relevant assets for me. I use generative AI primarily for ideations as said, usually i rely here on Firefly hub by Adobe where i have access to many AI models and also Firefly Boards where i do make some ideations and moodboards with AI and non-AI material. I also use Google Gemini Pro for ideations of some of my assets as well as stuff like game design inspiration etc. I do use genAI for more than that but it would be a much longer response (for example i sometimes use Motionmaker in Autodesk Maya or Autodesk Flow Studio for multiple purposes).

replies.author: Trashy_io
replies.body:
I think you should start by tracking how much time you spend on task, then once you have that data you can see where you are moving the slowest, and dive into that area and design a workflow yourself to solve that problem. Easier said than done but a little research and patiences you can pretty easily figure it out! 

I think that's where the real opportunity is bc most products & work flows are made and designed to be fitting for the general market and will just have you learning tool after tool as they come, vs creating ur custom tools for yourself snd agents that solves your specific problem/task (only if it is a long term re occurring problem/task) 

I think its pretty clear AI as a whole is plateauing as technology at the moment. So I didn't think there is much value being provided by new models or work flows that are similar to others already out there. I legit never used any of the models past 5.1 thinking and now its gone ;( but im not too sure they didn't just replace the .1 with a .4 feels way more similar after they removed 5.1 models XD

comments.author: Radiant_Mind33
comments.body:
It's a odd question, but i'll bite.

What can I say about my workflow? I can tell you that I absolutely cannot touch a free/low paid tier model for literally any task. Unless it's like some brainless data array entries. \*Maybe\* i'd let ChatGPT give me some pointers. THEN i'd have a pro model do the coding.

ChatGPT will maybe get through 1,000 lines of code. If you get some super lucky context memory drop MAYBE it will get through 5k lines once a month lmao.

My main game file is 15k lines of complex math and rendering...

replies.author: SlimPerceptions
replies.body: I hear you, but don’t you think if you broke down your tasks into more concrete and guided directives, even a flash/lite model could complete your tasks for you?

replies.author: Radiant_Mind33
replies.body:
Sure, but let's be clear on the differences between getting something to work and actually polishing that thing. Like you certainly can run the same task 10 times into a free model and get it down and polished. But by doing it 10 times you introduce context leaks, hallucinations, and that's all on top of model drift. If you are on a cloud model I mean. 

Conversely, the pro model will have the thing done and polished in 2 passes. Then you can literally play with it however you want. The task is done. Plus, visually the pro models are much better on single shots. Also, i could easily run a test through Claude free vs Gemini pro, but everyone knows what the results will be.

replies.author: ipreuss
replies.body:
Having a main file of 15 kLoC sounds just like bad design to me. Why would you do it that way?

I currently have a rule that a file with more than 500 LoC blocks approval.

replies.author: Radiant_Mind33
replies.body: My repo would have like 300 files if I did it your way. That is definitely not better.

replies.author: ipreuss
replies.body: Why would that not be better?

replies.author: odragora
replies.body:
It would be much, much better.

It's extremely common in professional software development to even enforce a limit on how many lines of code in a file can be, whether with a hard limit or with requiring to split huge files on modules during a code review. Otherwise the codebase quickly becomes a nightmare for the team.

replies.author: Radiant_Mind33
replies.body:
Lol, speak for yourself.

You think digging through 300 different files is easier than 1? 

Good luck

replies.author: odragora
replies.body: I speak from more than a decade of experience working as a software developer in different companies, this is how any serious team is working.

replies.author: Radiant_Mind33
replies.body:
Anyone can write that.

Explain what solo projects you worked on and how 300 file repos are so simple for you to keep track of. It sounds like someone else did most of the work and you were just there.

replies.author: ipreuss
replies.body: Get yourself educated about SOLID design principles, clean code and refactoring.

replies.author: ipreuss
replies.body: With the right abstractions, you don’t need to dig through them.

replies.author: ZuffaZombie
replies.body: Oh GAWD what a rats nest 😂🐀

comments.author: SlimPerceptions
comments.body: It can go as heavy as you want it to, with various trade-offs in efficiency. Don’t let someone convince you you should be using more agentic loops or less agentic loops. We are not yet at the point where agents can do it all autonomously, so find the workflows optimized for *you*. That’s the real answer.

comments.author: ivyentre
comments.body: You can develop or use AI as much as you please as long as you keep in mind that gaming fandom loathes AI right now and it doesn't appear that will change. I'm not sure if it's a vocal minority or the majority overall but the hate level is vitriolic right now.

replies.author: AgenticGameDev
replies.body: But also the AI slop games are flooding out. I made this game in 6 days, 1day...4h... And that is crap games. But yes I don't disagree.

replies.author: ivyentre
replies.body: The Anti crowd doesn't care for a difference between slop and quality. They hear AI and they tune out or attack. There is no middle ground; it's all slop to them.

comments.author: just_a_dev_3324
comments.body:
Ummmm well.... depends on how far your want to go

If you want to build a game with AI. This is a straight forward step... Pick an engine or (build one with AI) get the AI to write the code (eg. Claude/Codex). And have  AI build assets for you (meshy, leanardo ai etc.) and then get the AI string them up together thats what I did with my game fragged. I effectively had to work with the AI to get the end product done! This is very possible now [https://mercutio32.itch.io/fragged](https://mercutio32.itch.io/fragged) !

In the future we will basically be creating AI game studios:  
\- Define some AI agents that come up with high level game design documents based on your ideas.   
\- Build a pipeline of AI agents that take the GDD and build the game (just like you did in my first statement but more autonomous this time your not orchestrating the production the agents are)   
\- Iteratively improve the product and fix issues with the agents (sooner or later we will get agents with good enough computer use that will be able to play test the game and then it will be one big iterative feedback loop). 

Really we are not fully here yet but pretty sure by the end of the year we will get here give how autonomous agents are becoming.

comments.body:
I don't know if it is "current state of ai game dev" but I recorded my workflows as claude skills in my project 

I think what's different from what I am doing is I am not using an engine and I think AIs do really well with engines, but then you're constrained to what the engine offers, which is a lot and probably good enough and I just have control issues I guess.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body:
I use AI TDD. Great test coverage is also great acting as a specification that AI can ask...did I break any thing and how should this be used.... Also Modularization. Smaller modules of modules is important. AI is great working inside one module or with modules as building blocks but suck at a traditional 3 tier architecture...

Lastly use CC Teams and think like a some one who guide a awesome new hire. What IA don't know is on you....

But be prepared and USE GIT AND BACKUPS. AI can screw you really hard without blinking. Oh you did not like that let me revert back to beginning..... git reset --hard f2a4f32 (f2a4f32 = you first commit on the repo).

comments.author: SeekingSpire
comments.body:
In my limited experience and humble opinion, the biggest misconception about “AI game dev” is thinking the AI will just generate the game. In practice it’s more like this:

You spend part of your time building the game, and part of your time building tools that let your AI agents work effectively inside your project.

Most of the real productivity gains come from creating an environment where agents can read the repo, run builds/tests, modify files, and iterate. Once that loop works, they become extremely productive collaborators.

The other thing people should understand is that you rarely one-shot anything. The bigger the project, the more structure and tooling you need. AI is incredible at implementing scoped tasks, refactoring systems, and generating code — but it still needs constraints.

Cost-wise, if you’re seriously using coding agents today you’re probably spending a few hundred dollars a month. Routing usage smartly (and relying on OAuth access where possible) matters a lot.

The big shift in 2026 isn’t “AI making games.” It’s developers learning how to structure projects so AI can actually help build them.

You can check out my website to see how I've personally used AI in my first (and upcoming) projects and I'm happy to discuss/share any further details if my approach interests you at all.
